title: Python
tagline: From your first print to your first program. Each chapter: a short lesson, then exercises to check what you learned.

lesson.p: Python is a programming language: a way to write instructions that a computer can run. It is known for being easy to read, almost like plain English. People use it to build websites, analyse data, automate tasks and create artificial intelligence.
The print() function shows text on the screen. The text goes between quotes. We call it a string.
Python reads your program from top to bottom, one line after another. Each print() writes on a new line.
A line that starts with # is a comment. Python ignores it. Use it to explain your code to yourself or to others.

If you forget a quote, or if you write Print instead of print, Python shows an error message. This is not a failure. It is a clue that tells you what to fix. Python treats capital and small letters as different.

lesson.h: A variable is a box with a name
lesson.p: A variable keeps a piece of information so you can use it later. You create it with the = sign, which means "put this value in this box".
print(city) shows what is inside the variable. print("city") shows the word city itself, because it is text between quotes.

A variable name has no spaces, does not start with a digit and does not use a hyphen. Write it in small letters, with _ between words: my_age, total_price. Python treats capital and small letters as different: Age and age are two different variables.

Every value has a type. int: a whole number (12). float: a number with a decimal part, written with a decimal point (3.14). str: text ("Kribi"). bool: true or false (True or False). The type() function tells you the type of a value.

lesson.h: Changing a value, showing several things
lesson.p: You can give a variable a new value. The old one is forgotten. Also, print() can show several items separated by commas. It puts a space between them.

lesson.p: Python can calculate: + (addition), - (subtraction), * (multiplication), / (division), ** (power). As in maths, multiplication comes before addition. Brackets change the order.

/ always gives a number with a decimal part. // gives the whole part of the division. % gives the remainder. The remainder is very useful, for example to know if a number is even (remainder 0 when you divide by 2).
With text, + joins two texts together and * repeats a text. len() gives the number of characters.
Put an f before the quotes, then put the variables between curly brackets. It is the clearest way to show a sentence with values.
input() pauses the program and gets what the user types, always as text. To calculate with it, you must convert it: int() for a whole number, float() for a number with a decimal part.

lesson.p: Python can compare values. The result is always True or False. The comparisons are: == (equal), != (not equal), < , > , <= , >=. Be careful: = stores a value in a variable, but == compares two values.

With if, part of the code runs only if the condition is true. The line ends with a colon (:), and the lines that belong to it are moved to the right by 4 spaces. This is called indentation. In Python, it is required.

lesson.h: else and elif: the other cases
lesson.p: else runs when the condition is false. elif ("else if") lets you test several cases in order. Python stops at the first true case.
and: both conditions must be true. or: at least one must be true. not: reverses the result.
lesson.code:
print(True and False)
print(5 > 3 or 2 > 9)
print(not False)

lesson.p: Forgetting the colon at the end of the if line, or forgetting to indent the next line: Python shows an indentation error or a syntax error. Another trap: writing = instead of == in a condition.

lesson.h: for: repeat a known number of times
lesson.p: A loop repeats instructions. With for and range(n), the indented block runs n times. The variable i takes the values 0, 1, 2... up to n-1.

lesson.h: range(start, end): the end is excluded
lesson.p: range(1, 4) starts at 1 and stops before 4: 1, 2, 3. You can show the loop variable to see where you are.
A loop is often used to build a total. You start at 0 and add something on each turn.
lesson.code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total = total + i
print(total)

lesson.h: while: repeat as long as it is true
lesson.p: while repeats as long as the condition is true. Something must change inside the loop so that it ends one day. If not, it runs forever (an infinite loop).
lesson.code:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1

lesson.p: break stops the loop immediately, even if there were turns left.

lesson.h: Lists: several values in one variable
lesson.p: A list groups several values between square brackets. You get an item by its position, called the index. Be careful: the first item has index 0, and -1 means the last one.
append() adds an item at the end. A for loop can go through all the items of a list directly.
lesson.code:
fruits = ["mango", "pineapple"]
fruits.append("banana")
for f in fruits:
    print(f)

lesson.h: Functions: a block of code you can reuse
lesson.p: A function groups instructions under a name. You create it with def, with parameters between brackets, and then you call it when you need it.
lesson.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello", name)

greet("Awa")
greet("Paul")

lesson.p: print() shows something on the screen, but gives nothing to the rest of the program. return sends a value back to the place where the function was called. You can then store it or calculate with it.
With lists, loops, conditions and functions, you have the building blocks of almost every program. You can already write small useful tools.

lesson.p: 12 questions on the whole course: text, variables, calculations, conditions, loops, lists and functions. There are no hints. To pass, you must get at least 9 questions right on the first try. You can take it again as many times as you need. Take your time and read each program line by line, as Python would.
